name: Bigonial width

card.summary: Bigonial width is the distance between the two gonions (the outer corners of the lower jaw), a measure looksmaxxers use to judge how wide and square the jawline looks from the front and to decide whether jaw-widening steps could improve facial balance.
card.note: A measurement concept, not a treatment; the procedures people use to change it (implants, filler, masseter botulinum toxin, orthognathic surgery) carry their own risks.

quick.overview:
Bigonial width is the straight-line distance between the left and right gonion, the point at each lower-jaw corner where the horizontal body of the mandible meets the vertical ramus. In looksmaxxing communities it is read as how wide the lower face looks in a front-on photo, usually compared with the width across the cheekbones (bizygomatic or interzygomatic width).

Forum members describe a jaw that is wide relative to the cheekbones as looking more masculine, square and balanced, and a narrow one as making the face look top-heavy. Anatomical research measures the same distance mainly for forensic sex estimation and in studies of aging and of masseter-reducing treatments.
quick.how: People assess it from a front-facing photo or a radiograph, often as a ratio to cheekbone width. Those who want a wider or more defined jaw discuss jaw-angle implants, jawline filler, or orthognathic surgery, while those with a prominent jaw from large masseter muscles discuss botulinum toxin to narrow it. Some forum members ask whether chewing or muscle training widens the jaw; research on that question is limited. Photo angle and grooming are also discussed as ways of presenting a narrower jaw differently.
quick.risks: Measuring bigonial width carries no risk in itself. The procedures associated with changing it are medical interventions with their own complications, such as swelling, asymmetry, nerve injury, infection or the need for repeat treatment, and are performed by licensed clinicians. Do-it-yourself injection posts on forums are the subject of safety concerns from clinicians generally.

lead: Bigonial width (often abbreviated BGW) is the distance between the two gonions, the outer lower corners of the jaw where the mandibular body turns upward into the ramus. [1] It is a standard anthropometric and radiographic measurement, and in looksmaxxing culture it is treated as a key determinant of how wide and structured the lower face appears from the front. [2]

Forum members who study facial proportions compare bigonial width with the width across the cheekbones. A jaw that is close to cheekbone width is described as looking robust and masculine, while a much narrower one is described as giving a top-heavy or less photogenic frontal view. [3][4] The same threads say other features, such as ramus height, chin height and large masseter muscles, can partly compensate.

Published research uses the measurement mostly outside aesthetics: forensic anthropology studies report that bigonial width differs significantly between sexes, [5][6] and anatomical studies describe how the mandible changes with age. [7][8] A separate literature examines how botulinum toxin injected into the masseter reduces lower-face width. [9]

chain: Measure the distance between the jaw corners
Compare it with cheekbone width in a front view

angle.text: Bigonial width is a way of describing how wide the lower face looks from the front. People who want a more square, masculine or balanced frontal profile use it to decide whether to widen the jaw, and people with very prominent jaw angles use it to discuss slimming options.

paras: The gonion is the landmark at the outermost, lowest and rearmost point of the mandibular angle, where the ramus meets the body. [1] Bigonial width is the straight distance between the left and right gonions. It can be measured on a skull, on a panoramic dental radiograph or CT scan, with 3D imaging, or approximated from a front-view photograph. [6]

Looksmaxxing communities usually express it relative to another width, most often the bizygomatic width, and some discussions debate a particular ideal ratio. [3][10] Related terms in the same discussions include gonial angle, ramus length and facial width-to-height ratio.

Proponents of the concept argue that bigonial width determines how wide the lower jaw looks from the front, and that a low value relative to the cheekbones can make the lower face look narrow, particularly with a short chin. [3][4] They describe a wide value as making the jaw look more masculine and square when ramus length, gonial angle and facial width-to-height ratio are also adequate. [3]

Some members consider it more important than ramus length or gonial angle for frontal harmony, while others say it matters less than side-profile features. Several threads discuss presenting a narrow jaw with three-quarter photo angles instead of full-frontal portraits. [11]

Forensic reviews report that bigonial width, along with condylar and coronoid height and coronion-gonion distance, shows significant sexual dimorphism in the mandible. [5] A systematic review and meta-analysis of mandibular parameters for sex determination covered 2,385 individuals in nine studies. [1] A study of 600 panoramic radiographs likewise used bigonial width among seven mandibular measures to separate male and female patients. [6]

Imaging studies of the aging face describe changes in mandibular dimensions with age, including effects on jaw angle and the lower face, with implications for aesthetic treatment. [7][8] A dental-school study examined how gonial angle, ramus height and bigonial width correlate with age and sex in dentate subjects. [12]

Forum discussions note that the main routes to a wider bony jaw are surgical, such as jaw-angle implants, and some members describe implants as the only way to increase it. [3] Filler along the jaw angle is another approach people discuss for adding width or definition, and some forum members have posted about administering it themselves, which clinicians generally advise against. Corrective jaw surgery (orthognathic surgery) changes mandibular position and can alter frontal soft-tissue dimensions. [13]

In the other direction, botulinum toxin injected into the masseter muscle is used clinically to reduce lower-face width. A systematic review of 20 publications reported that it lowered bigonial width by reducing masseter volume, with follow-up of 3 to 48 months, and noted that repeat treatment at intervals is advisable to maintain the result. [9]

Some forum threads ask whether chewing or jaw exercise increases jaw width, and others whether jaw width changes after age 18. [14][15] No clinical trial cited here has tested chewing exercises for bigonial width.

No clinical trials have tested bigonial width as a predictor of perceived attractiveness in the way forum theories describe it. Related human research includes the systematic review of botulinum toxin in the masseter for reducing bigonial width (20 publications, all but one prospective, follow-up 3 to 48 months), [9] radiographic and forensic studies of its sex differences, [1][5][6] and imaging studies of mandibular aging. [7][8]

lore.intro: Bigonial width is discussed on looksmax.org as an under-appreciated factor in frontal facial harmony, usually alongside ramus length, gonial angle and cheekbone width. [3][4]

claims.claim: Bigonial width is a key factor in facial attractiveness and harmony
claims.believers: Thread authors say it sets how wide the lower jaw looks from the front and can make or break the frontal view, and that a width close to the cheekbones looks masculine and robust. [3][4]
claims.experts: Published research on bigonial width concerns sex differences and anatomy rather than attractiveness ratings; no cited study tests the claim directly. [5][6]

claims.claim: Low bigonial width relative to cheekbone width makes the face look top-heavy
claims.believers: Members describe a narrow jaw under wide cheekbones as unbalanced, particularly with a short chin, and say large masseters or a tall chin can offset it. [3]
claims.experts: Facial aging and mandible studies describe measurable changes in the lower face that affect appearance, but they do not evaluate this ratio. [7][8]

claims.claim: Implants (or filler) are the way to increase bigonial width
claims.believers: Posters say implants are the only route to a wider bony jaw and discuss filler as a way to add width. [3]
claims.experts: Clinical literature describes surgical and injectable contouring in general; the cited research on width change focuses on masseter reduction with botulinum toxin and on orthognathic surgery. [9][13]

claims.believers: Threads debate whether chewing or hard-food regimens increase jaw width, with some members reporting changes and others disputing them. [14]
claims.experts: No clinical study cited here has examined chewing exercise and bigonial width.
